mainTopic: Conduct in בית דין: who stands and sits, honoring a תלמיד חכם while keeping the court fair, and judges' duties learned from ״מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק״.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier question with a second answer: רב יוסף told רב נחמן that עולא was a תלמיד חכם because it matters when a case is decided by שודא דדייני. Next it narrows the argument between the חכמים and רבי יהודה about standing in court. עולא says עדים always stand. רב הונא says that at גמר דין the judges sit and the בעלי דינין stand, and a second version gives a different source for this. Stories follow about honoring a תלמיד חכם in court without making the other side feel the judge is biased: רב נחמן and the duck, and רב פפא and the court's agent. רבה בר רב הונא gives rules for a צורבא מרבנן who has a case with an עם הארץ. He also rules that a scholar need not testify before a lesser judge, but only in money matters and never where there is חילול ה׳. אמימר seats all the witnesses for רב יימר, explaining that the עשה of כבוד התורה outweighs the עשה of witnesses standing. Finally, after a סימן, a ברייתא begins listing rules for judges learned from ״מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק״, and this list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A second reason: judicial discretion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives another reason why רב יוסף told רב נחמן that עולא was a תלמיד חכם: for cases decided by שודא דדייני.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else: it matters for cases decided by the judges' discretion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an earlier question: why did רב יוסף bother telling רב נחמן that עולא was a Torah scholar? It now offers a second possible reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes the evidence cannot settle a case, and the judges must decide by their own sense of the matter (שודא דדייני). In such a case, knowing that one side is a תלמיד חכם could tilt the decision in his favor. This is a new, alternative answer to the same question.

keyTerms.meaning: Or else / alternatively; it brings a second answer
Judicial discretion: the judges decide by their own judgment when the evidence cannot settle the case

phrases.english: Alternatively, for the discretion of the judges.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to a question asked just before this section, about why רב יוסף sent word that עולא was a תלמיד חכם.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without an answer, it seems pointless for רב יוסף to tell a judge that one of the litigants is a scholar.
steps.terutzMaskana: It matters when the case must be decided by שודא דדייני, where the judges may lean toward the תלמיד חכם.

steps.title: עולא: the argument is only about litigants; witnesses always stand
steps.stepSummary: עולא limits the argument over standing in court to the בעלי דינין. עדים must stand according to everyone, based on the פסוק ״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: The argument is about the litigants. But about witnesses, everyone agrees they stand, as it says: "And the two men shall stand."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the argument between the חכמים (litigants must stand) and רבי יהודה (they may both be seated). עולא says this argument is only about the litigants, not the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא narrows the scope of the argument. For עדים there is no argument at all: they must stand when they testify, because the פסוק ״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״ is read as talking about witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: The litigants, the two sides in a court case

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the pattern for this whole section: each אמורא shows where the argument stops and where everyone agrees.

phrases.english: Ulla said: The dispute is about the litigants;
phrases.notes: This is the argument between the חכמים and רבי יהודה over whether litigants must stand in court.

phrases.english: but about witnesses, everyone agrees they are standing,
as it is written: "And the two men shall stand."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how far the argument over standing in court reaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument about standing applies only to בעלי דינין. All agree that עדים testify standing.

steps.title: רב הונא: the argument is only during the deliberation, not at the verdict
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא limits the argument to the משא ומתן stage. At גמר דין everyone agrees the judges sit and the litigants stand, learned from משה sitting and the people standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: The argument is during the discussion of the case. But at the verdict, everyone agrees the judges sit and the litigants stand, as it says: "And משה sat to judge the people, and the people stood."
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a different limit to the argument: it depends on the stage of the case, not on who the person is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the case is being argued (משא ומתן), the חכמים and רבי יהודה disagree about whether litigants stand. But when the verdict is given (גמר דין), all agree: judges sit and litigants stand. The source is the פסוק about משה judging the people while they stood.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'give and take': the stage when the case is being argued and discussed

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: מַחְלוֹקֶת בִּשְׁעַת מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן;
phrases.english: Rav Huna said: The dispute is at the time of the deliberation;
but at the time of the verdict,
everyone agrees the judges are sitting
and the litigants are standing,
as it is written: "And Moses sat to judge the people
and the people stood."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: מַחְלוֹקֶת בִּשְׁעַת מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second way of narrowing the same argument. עולא limited it by who stands; רב הונא limits it by when.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument applies only during משא ומתן. At גמר דין all agree: judges sit and litigants stand.

steps.title: Second version of רב הונא: the source is the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: A לישנא אחרינא gives רב הונא the same ruling but a different source: testimony is like the verdict stage, and witnesses must stand, so litigants stand at the verdict.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: The argument is during the discussion. But at the verdict, everyone agrees the judges sit and the litigants stand, because witnesses are like the verdict stage, and about them it says: "And the two men shall stand."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of רב הונא's statement. The ruling is the same, but the proof is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the proof is not the פסוק about משה. Instead: the testimony of עדים is compared to the stage of גמר דין, and the Torah says the witnesses stand (״וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים״). So the verdict stage also calls for standing.

keyTerms.meaning: Another version of the same statement
They are like the verdict stage

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ruling. The הלכה is exactly the same as in step 3; only the source in the פסוקים changes.
steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees that עדים stand and that at גמר דין the judges sit and the litigants stand. The argument between the חכמים and רבי יהודה is only about litigants during משא ומתן.

phrases.aramaic: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: מַחְלוֹקֶת בִּשְׁעַת מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן,
phrases.english: Another version: The dispute is at the time of the deliberation,
but at the time of the verdict,
everyone agrees the judges are sitting
and the litigants are standing;
since witnesses are like the verdict stage,
and it is written about them: "And the two men shall stand."

steps.triggerLanguage: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: מַחְלוֹקֶת בִּשְׁעַת מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats רב הונא's ruling from step 3 but replaces the פסוק about משה with the פסוק about witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Same ruling as step 3; the source is that testimony is like גמר דין, and witnesses stand.

steps.title: רב נחמן's dilemma: should he stand for רב הונא's wife?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא's wife has a case before רב נחמן. Standing for her could scare off the other side; not standing would fail to honor her, since אשת חבר הרי היא כחבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא's wife had a case before רב נחמן. He said: What should I do? If I stand up for her, the other side will be too scared to argue. If I don't stand up for her, the wife of a scholar is like a scholar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows a real conflict about honor in court. רב נחמן is stuck between two duties.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On one side, the other litigant may think the judge favors her and keep quiet about his claims. On the other side, the wife of a חבר deserves the same honor as the חבר himself, so he really should stand.

keyTerms.meaning: His claims will be shut down: he will be too intimidated to argue
The wife of a scholar is treated like the scholar himself

phrases.english: The wife of Rav Huna

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה לַהּ דִּינָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: had a case before Rav Nachman,
He said: What should we do?
If I stand up before her,
the claims of the other litigant will be shut down.
If I don't stand up before her,
the wife of a scholar is like a scholar.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵיתְהוּ דְּרַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לַהּ דִּינָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the rules of standing in court to a story about honor and fairness inside בית דין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can a judge honor a תלמיד חכם's wife who is a litigant without scaring off the other side?

steps.title: The solution: a duck thrown on רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן tells his attendant to make a duck fly onto him, so he can stand up in a way that looks accidental.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to his attendant: Go out, make a duck fly at me and throw it on me, and I'll stand up.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן solves his problem with a clever trick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By standing up because a duck landed on him, he really stands for רב הונא's wife and gives her the honor she deserves. But to the other litigant it looks like he stood only because of the duck, so no one thinks he is favoring her.
steps.whatToRemember: A judge must keep both sides feeling equal in court, even while giving proper honor to a תלמיד חכם and his family.

phrases.english: He said to his attendant:
Go out and make a duck fly at me
and throw it on me, and I will stand up.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְשַׁמָּעֵיהּ: צֵא וְאַפְרַח עֲלַי בַּר אֲוָוזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the dilemma raised in step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Stand up in a way that looks accidental (because of the duck), so honor is given without hurting the other litigant.

steps.title: How could the judge stand if litigants must stand at the verdict?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the duck plan using רב הונא's rule that at גמר דין the judges sit and the litigants stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't the Master say: the argument is only during the discussion of the case, but at the final verdict everyone agrees the judges sit and the litigants stand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the story of רב נחמן standing up for רב הונא's wife. It quotes רב הונא's own rule from step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the verdict the judge must be sitting and the litigants standing. If רב נחמן stood up for her, the judge would be standing, which seems to break the rule that judges sit at the verdict.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't the Master say (a challenge from a known statement)
The discussion stage of a court case

phrases.english: But didn't the Master say:
phrases.notes: The Master here is רב הונא, quoting his rule from earlier on this דף.

phrases.english: The dispute is during the discussion of the case,
but at the time of the final verdict
everyone agrees the judges are sitting
and the litigants are standing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's plan of standing up, from step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן standing up for רב הונא's wife
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: At גמר דין judges must sit and litigants stand; a standing judge goes against this

steps.title: The judge half-sits while giving the verdict
steps.stepSummary: The judge sits like someone bending to untie his shoe, neither fully standing nor fully sitting, and announces the verdict.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sits like someone untying his shoe, and says: 'So-and-so, you are innocent; so-and-so, you are liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the judge takes a half-sitting position while giving the verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This in-between position lets the judge keep the honor he showed her and still give the verdict from a seated posture. So both needs are handled at once.

keyTerms.meaning: Like someone untying his shoe (a half-sitting position)

phrases.english: He sits like someone untying his shoe,
and says: "So-and-so, you are innocent,"
"So-and-so, you are liable."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical method that satisfies both requirements
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Standing for her would break the rule that judges sit at גמר דין
steps.terutzMaskana: A half-sitting posture lets the judge give the verdict properly
steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן honored רב הונא's wife with a 'duck' excuse to stand, and gave the verdict in a half-sitting position so the court rules stayed intact.

steps.title: Seating both a Torah scholar and an unlearned litigant
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא rules that the court seats the צורבא מרבנן and also tells the עם הארץ to sit; if he chooses to stand, that is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a Torah scholar and an unlearned person have a case together, we seat the scholar and also tell the unlearned person 'Sit.' If he stands anyway, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins about a case between a young Torah scholar and an unlearned person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court may seat the scholar out of honor, but it must offer the same seat to the other side so things stay equal. If the unlearned person stands on his own out of respect, the court does not have to stop him.

keyTerms.meaning: We have no problem with it

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
This Torah scholar and an unlearned person
who have a court case with each other:
we seat the Torah scholar,
and to the unlearned person we also say "Sit";
and if he stands, we have no problem with it.
phrases.notes: He means the unlearned person, if he decides to stand out of respect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new related topic: honoring a scholar in court while staying fair
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seat the scholar, offer a seat to the עם הארץ too; if he stands by choice, it is fine

steps.title: The story of רב בר שרביא in רב פפא's court
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא seated both sides, but the court's agent kicked the unlearned man and made him stand, and רב פפא did not tell him to sit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב בר שרביא had a case before רב פפא. רב פפא seated him and also seated the other side. The court's agent came, kicked the unlearned man and made him stand, and רב פפא did not tell him 'Sit.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that seems to fit the rule at first, then raises a problem. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא followed the rule by seating both. But when the agent forced the unlearned man to stand, רב פפא stayed silent, which looks like it favors the scholar.

keyTerms.meaning: The opposing party in a case

phrases.aramaic: רַב בַּר שֵׁרֵבְיָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ דִּינָא
phrases.english: Rav bar Sherevya had a court case
before Rav Pappa.
He seated him and also seated his opponent.
The court's agent came,
kicked him and made the unlearned man stand,
and Rav Pappa did not say to him "Sit."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב בַּר שֵׁרֵבְיָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ דִּינָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story applying the rule of step 9
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge seated both sides; the agent stood the עם הארץ up and the judge did not object

steps.title: Wouldn't the unlearned man feel he can't argue his case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב פפא could stay silent, since the unlearned man would feel the court is against him and hold back his claims.
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he do that? But the man's claims would get shut down!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's silence in the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one side sits and the other is forced to stand, the standing side may feel the judge favors his opponent. Then he might be too scared to argue fully, which makes the trial unfair.

phrases.english: How could he do this?
But his claims get shut down!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי עָבֵיד הָכִי? וְהָא מִסְתַּתְּמָן טַעֲנָתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's conduct in step 10
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא not telling the עם הארץ to sit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Unequal treatment makes a litigant feel the judge is biased, so he won't argue fully

steps.title: The unlearned man blames the agent, not the judge
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא reasoned that the man would think the judge seated him and only the agent was upset with him, so he would not feel the judge was biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: He will say, 'The judge did seat me; it's the agent who isn't happy with me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with רב פפא's own reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is how the litigant sees the judge. Since רב פפא himself seated him, the man knows the judge is fair, and he blames only the agent.

keyTerms.meaning: He will say (this is how he will think)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
He will say,
phrases.notes: "He" is the unlearned man who was made to stand.

phrases.english: "He did seat me;
phrases.notes: "He" here is the judge, רב פפא.

phrases.english: it's the agent who isn't pleased with me."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being made to stand would make the man think the judge is biased
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the judge seated him, he blames only the agent, so his claims are not shut down
steps.whatToRemember: Fairness in court depends on how the litigant sees the judge. If the judge treated him equally, a rude agent does not make the court look biased.

steps.title: The scholar should not come early and sit with the judge
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא rules that a צורבא מרבנן with a case against an עם הארץ should not arrive early and sit with the judge, since it looks like he is preparing his case with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה בר רב הונא said: When a Torah scholar and an unlearned person have a case together, the scholar should not come early and sit, because it looks like he is setting up his case with the judge.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching from רבה בר רב הונא about the same kind of case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the scholar just wants to learn with the judge, sitting with him before the trial looks like he is planning his case with the judge. That appearance is a problem on its own.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
This Torah scholar and an unlearned person
who have a court case with each other:
the Torah scholar should not come early and sit,
because it looks
like someone setting up his case with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second rule from the same אמורא on the same type of case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A scholar-litigant should not sit early with the judge, because it looks like he is planning his case

steps.title: Exception: a scholar with a regular learning time
steps.stepSummary: The rule applies only when the scholar has no fixed time to learn with the judge; if he does, it is fine, since everyone knows he is there for his regular learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when he does not have a set time. But if he has a set time, we have no problem with it, because the other side will say: 'He is busy with his regular learning time.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the rule of step 13 with an exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem in step 13 was only how it looks. If the scholar always sits with the judge at that hour, the other side will see it as his usual learning and not as planning the case.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when (a limiting phrase)
He has a fixed, regular time

phrases.english: And we only said this
where he does not have a set time,
but if he has a set time,
we have no problem with it;
he will say: "He is busy with his regular time."
phrases.notes: "He will say" means the other litigant, who sees the scholar there.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא קְבִיעַ לֵיהּ עִידָּנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 13
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the scholar has a fixed learning time with the judge, sitting early is allowed
steps.whatToRemember: A צורבא מרבנן in a case should not sit early with the judge, since it looks like planning the case. If that is his regular learning time, it is fine, because nobody will think it is about the case.
steps.whyThisMatters: Throughout this section, the court cares about how things look to the other side. A judge must not only be fair, but be seen as fair.

steps.title: A scholar need not testify before a lesser judge
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא rules that a צורבא מרבנן who knows testimony does not have to go testify before a judge lesser than him if it would be beneath his dignity.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה בר רב הונא said: A Torah scholar who knows testimony, but it is demeaning for him to go to the court of a judge who is lesser than him to testify before him, should not go.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא gives another rule about a צורבא מרבנן. If testifying in front of a less important judge would lower his dignity, he does not have to go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steps before were about a scholar who is himself one of the sides in a case. Now the case is a scholar who is only a witness. His honor as a Torah scholar can excuse him from coming to testify.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a demeaning thing for him

phrases.english: And Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
A Torah scholar who knows testimony,
and it is a demeaning matter for him
to go to the court of a judge who is lesser than him
to testify before him – he should not go.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from the same אמורא (רבה בר רב הונא) about a scholar's dignity in court, now as a witness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A צורבא מרבנן does not have to testify before a lesser judge if it is demeaning to him.

steps.title: Support from the law of returning lost objects
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי shows that a משנה already teaches this: someone who would not normally carry a sack or basket does not have to pick it up to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said: We also learned this in a משנה: If someone found a sack or a basket, and it is not his way to carry such things, he does not have to take it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא brings a proof for רבה בר רב הונא's rule from a משנה about returning lost objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: השבת אבידה is a real מצוה, yet a person who would not normally carry a sack is excused from it, because of his dignity. In the same way, a scholar's dignity can excuse him from the מצוה of testifying.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not his way to take (carry) it

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי,
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said:
We too learned this in a mishna:
phrases.notes: The משנה is in בבא מציעא 29b, in the laws of returning lost objects.

phrases.english: If one found a sack or a basket

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין דַּרְכּוֹ לִיטּוֹל – הֲרֵי זֶה לֹא יִטּוֹל.
phrases.english: and it is not his way to take it – he does not take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source from a משנה to support the ruling of step 15.
steps.raayaObject: רבה בר רב הונא's rule that a scholar's dignity excuses him from testifying before a lesser judge.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא מציעא: one whose dignity does not allow him to carry a sack or basket is excused from returning it.

steps.title: Dignity counts only in money matters, not when there is חילול ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the rule: a scholar's dignity counts only in money matters. Where there is a prohibition or חילול ה׳, a rabbi's honor is set aside.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to money matters. But in matters of prohibition, the פסוק says: "There is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against ה׳." Wherever there is desecration of ה׳'s name, we do not give honor to the rabbi.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets a limit on the rule just taught. Dignity can excuse a scholar only in money cases, not where keeping it would lead to an איסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Missing testimony in a money case only affects money, so the scholar's honor can come first. When an איסור is involved, honoring a person cannot outweigh honoring ה׳. The פסוק teaches that no human consideration stands against ה׳.
steps.whatToRemember: A scholar's honor can excuse him in money matters, but never when there is an איסור or חילול ה׳.

phrases.english: This applies only to monetary matters,
but in matters of prohibition –
"There is neither wisdom nor understanding
nor counsel against the Lord";

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ חִלּוּל ה׳ –
phrases.english: wherever there is desecration of the name of the Lord –
we do not show honor to the teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of steps 15-16 to money matters.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dignity exemption applies only in money matters; where there is חילול ה׳, a rabbi's honor is not considered.

steps.title: אמימר seats all the witnesses for רב יימר
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר came to testify for מר זוטרא before אמימר, and אמימר seated all the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר knew testimony for מר זוטרא. He came before אמימר, and אמימר seated all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a scholar who came to testify. The judge, אמימר, let all the witnesses sit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the scholar did go to testify. אמימר honored him by letting him sit, and seated the other witnesses too, so not only one of them would sit. This sets up רב אשי's challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: Rav Yeimar knew
testimony for Mar Zutra.
He came before Ameimar,
who seated all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יֵימַר הֲוָה יָדַע לֵיהּ סָהֲדוּתָא לְמָר זוּטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story about a scholar who testifies, continuing the theme of a scholar's honor in court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אמימר seated all the witnesses because a Torah scholar was among them.

steps.title: רב אשי: witnesses must stand
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי challenges אמימר using עולא's rule that everyone agrees witnesses must stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to אמימר: But didn't עולא say that the argument is only about the sides in the case, but about witnesses everyone agrees they stand?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks אמימר how he could let the witnesses sit, since עולא taught that witnesses must stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an argument about whether the sides in a case must stand. עולא says that argument does not apply to witnesses. Everyone agrees witnesses stand, so seating them seems to break the law.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (opening a challenge)
The sides in a court case

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Ameimar:
But didn't Ulla say:
The dispute is about the litigants,
but regarding witnesses, everyone agrees they stand!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אמימר's action in step 18.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to עולא, witnesses must stand, and everyone agrees. So letting them sit goes against the הלכה.

steps.title: כבוד התורה outweighs witnesses standing
steps.stepSummary: אמימר answers that standing is a עשה and honoring Torah is also a עשה, and the עשה of כבוד התורה comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is a positive commandment and that is a positive commandment, and the positive commandment of honoring the Torah comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר defends what he did. Two מצוות עשה clash here, and honoring the Torah wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אמימר agrees that witnesses should stand, and calls it a עשה. But honoring a Torah scholar is also a עשה. When they clash, כבוד התורה is stronger, so the scholar may sit, and the other witnesses sit along with him.
steps.whatToRemember: When the עשה of witnesses standing clashes with the עשה of כבוד התורה, כבוד התורה comes first.

phrases.english: He said to him:
This is a positive מצוה and that is a positive מצוה,
phrases.notes: The first is witnesses standing; the second is honoring a Torah scholar.

phrases.english: and the positive מצוה of honoring the Torah takes precedence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge from step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Weighing two מצוות עשה against each other
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Witnesses must always stand, so seating them is wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: Standing is only a עשה, and the עשה of כבוד התורה outweighs it, so the scholar may be seated.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming discussions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן, four key words to help remember the order of the teachings that come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: (Memory aid: advocate, ignoramus, robbery, fraud)
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new teaching. The גמרא is setting up the next section with a list of key words for remembering what comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word hints at one of the upcoming teachings, in order. It works like a table of contents for the next part of the סוגיא.

phrases.english: (Mnemonic: advocate, ignoramus,
robbery, fraud)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A transition line that sets up the next set of teachings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling; it is a memory aid for the coming teachings.

steps.title: A judge must not defend his own mistaken rulings
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a דיין should not argue in defense of his own words, based on ״מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק״.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Where do we learn that a judge should not act as a defense lawyer for his own words? The verse says: 'Distance yourself from a false matter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה. Its first rule is that a דיין should not keep arguing to justify his own ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a דיין has said something, it is tempting to find reasons to prove he was right. The ברייתא says that defending your own words this way can lead you away from the truth. So the פסוק about staying far from falsehood forbids it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we learn this?
A defense lawyer, someone who argues for one side
Distance yourself from a false matter

steps.whyThisMatters: This פסוק becomes the source for every rule in the list that follows.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
From where do we learn for a judge
that he should not make himself a defense lawyer for his own words?
The verse teaches: "Distance yourself from a false matter."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the series of teachings that the סימן in step 21 was meant to help us remember.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דיין may not argue in defense of his own words. The source is ״מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק״.

steps.title: No ignorant student should sit before the judge
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: a דיין should not let an ignorant student sit before him. The source is the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where do we learn that an ignorant student should not sit before a judge? The verse says: 'Distance yourself from a false matter.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second rule in the ברייתא. A דיין should not have an unlearned student sitting before him during the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger now comes from someone else, not from the judge himself. An unlearned student may say wrong things that push the judge toward a mistake. The same פסוק covers this too.

phrases.english: And from where do we learn for a judge
that an ignorant student should not sit before him?
The verse teaches: "Distance yourself from a false matter."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִנַּיִן לַדַּיָּין שֶׁלֹּא יֵשֵׁב תַּלְמִיד בּוּר לְפָנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second item in the same list, using the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דיין should not let an ignorant student sit before him.

steps.title: Do not join a partner you know is a robber
steps.stepSummary: A דיין who knows his fellow דיין is a גזלן, and an עד who knows his fellow עד is a גזלן, should not join with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do we learn that a judge who knows his colleague is a robber, and likewise a witness who knows his fellow witness is a robber, should not join together with him? The verse says: 'Distance yourself from a false matter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The third rule covers both judges and witnesses. If you know your partner is a גזלן, do not team up with him on the case or the testimony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if nobody else knows, a person who knows his partner is a גזלן may not sit with him on a בית דין or testify alongside him. Joining him would make the ruling or the testimony rest on someone who should not count. That counts as being part of a 'false matter'.

keyTerms.meaning: Join together with, be counted with

phrases.english: From where do we learn for a judge who knows about his colleague
that he is a robber,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן עֵד שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ בַּחֲבֵירוֹ שֶׁהוּא גַּזְלָן –
phrases.english: and likewise a witness who knows about his fellow that he is a robber —
from where do we learn that he should not join together with him?
phrases.notes: A judge joins him to make up the court, and a witness joins him to make a pair of witnesses.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "Distance yourself from a false matter."

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִן לַדַּיָּין שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ לַחֲבֵירוֹ שֶׁהוּא גַּזְלָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third item in the list. It extends the rule to witnesses as well as judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דיין or עד who knows his partner is a גזלן may not join with him.

steps.title: A judge who senses the case is a fraud
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא begins the case of a דיין who knows a case is fraudulent but is tempted to rule anyway because the witnesses testified. The sentence continues past this point.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do we learn that a judge who knows a case is fraudulent should not say: 'Since the witnesses are testifying, I will decide it, and let…'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the fourth rule. It describes a judge's tempting excuse; the rest of his words and the source continue on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the judge senses the case is a trick, even though the עדים seem to support it. He is tempted to rule on their testimony and let the blame fall on them. The ברייתא is about to say this is forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the judge's thinking here is approved. This is the excuse the ברייתא is about to reject.

phrases.english: From where do we learn for a judge who knows about the case
that it is fraudulent,
that he should not say:
Since the witnesses are testifying —
I will decide it, and let…

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִן לַדַּיָּין שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ בַּדִּין שֶׁהוּא מְרוּמֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The fourth item in the list. It moves from who sits with the judge to how the judge handles a case he suspects is fraudulent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דיין who knows a case is fraudulent may not rule on it just because עדים testified. The rest of this rule continues on the next amud.
